<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|adorable|81|adorsed}}</noinclude>manding adoration; worthy of being adored; worthy of divine honors.
{{smaller block|There are those who have treated the history of Abraham as an astronomical record, and have spoken of our ''adorable'' Saviour as the sun in Aries.
{{right|''J. H. Newman'', Gram. of Assent, p. 364.}}}}
'''2.''' Worthy of the utmost love or admiration: as, she is an ''adorable'' creature; an ''adorable'' statue.
{{smaller block|When he [the pope] touched, as he did briefly, on the misfortunes of the church, an ''adorable'' fire came into his eyes.
{{right|''T. B. Aldrich'', Ponkapog to Pesth, p. 114.}}}}

'''adorableness''' (a̤-dōr′a̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The quality of being adorable, or worthy of adoration.

'''adorably''' (a̤-dōr′a̤-bli), ''adv.'' In a manner worthy of adoration.

'''adoral''' (ad-ō′ra̤l), ''a.''   [< L. ''ad'', to, + ''os'' (''ōr-''), mouth, + ''-al''; after ''aboral.'']   In ''zoöl.'', situated at or near the mouth; being relatively toward the mouth: the opposite of ''aboral.''
{{smaller block|They [''Halteriæ''] have a spiral ''adoral'' wreath of cilia for swimming.
{{right|''Stand. Nat. Hist.'', I. 43.}}}}
{{smaller block|The object of the unique, one-sided arrangement of the ''adoral'' cilia is to direct food-particles to the mouth.
{{right|''Amer. Jour. of Sci.'', 3d ser., XXIX. 328.}}}}

'''adorally''' (ad-ō′ra̤l-i), ''adv.'' Toward or in the direction of the mouth.

'''adoration''' (ad-ọ̄-rā′shọn), ''n.''   [< F. ''adoration'', < L. ''adoratio(n-)'', < ''adorare'': see ''adore''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' The act of paying honors, as to a divine being; worship addressed to a deity; the supreme worship due to God alone. {{smaller|[Sometimes used specifically of words addressed to the Deity expressive of a sense of his infinite holiness and perfection.] In the ''Rom. Cath. Ch.'', ''adoration'' is applied to any one of three kinds of worship (though properly only to the first), namely: ''latria'', or worship due to God alone; ''dulia'', or the secondary worship paid to angels and saints directly, or through the veneration of relics and images; and ''hyperdulia'', the higher worship paid to the Virgin Mary. The saints and the Virgin are adored as the friends of God, having intercessory power with him.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Lowly reverent
Towards either throne they bow, and to the ground
With solemn ''adoration'' down they cast
Their crowns.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iii. 351.}}}}
{{smaller block|Knowledge is the fire of ''adoration, adoration'' is the gate of knowledge.
{{right|''Bushnell'', Sermons for New Life, p. 163.}}}}
{{smaller block|They [Indians] perform their ''adorations'' and conjurations in the general language before spoken of, as the Catholics of all nations do their mass in the Latin.
{{right|''Beverley'', Virginia, iii. ¶ 31.}}}}

'''2.''' Homage, or an act of homage, paid to one in high place or held in high esteem; profound reverence; the utmost respect, regard, or esteem; the highest degree of love, as of a man for a woman; heart’s devotion.
{{smaller block|<poem>''Oli.'' How does he love me?
''Vio.'' With ''adorations'', with fertile tears,
With groans that thunder love, with sighs of fire.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., i. 5.}}}}

'''3.''' In ''art'' and ''archæol.'': (''a'') A representation of the adoration of the infant Jesus by the magi or the shepherds. (''b'') {{img float|file=century v01 p0107 c1f1.png|width=212px|align=right|cap={{smaller|An ancient Adoration.—Coin of Ephesus struck under Macrinus; British Museum. (Size of the original.)}}}} A representation of the worship of an ancient divinity, of the deified dead, or of a king or an emperor. In Latin, ''adoratio.'' {{smaller|Such representations are common in Greek vase-paintings and funeral sculptures, and in Roman reliefs and medals. The ancient adoration is usually characterized by the gesture of raising the right hand, particularly with the thumb laid on the first finger; though it is sometimes exhibited, chiefly in Oriental examples, in a prostrate position.}}

'''4.''' A method of electing a pope. See extract.
{{smaller block|The third way of creating Popes is by ''Adoration,'' which is perform’d in this manner: That Cardinal who . . . desires to favour any other Cardinal . . . puts himself before him in the Chappel, and makes him a low Reverence; and when it falls out that two thirds of the Cardinals do the same, the Pope is then understood to be created.
{{right|''G. H.'', tr. of Hist. Cardinals, III. 286. (''N. E. D.'')}}}}

{{smaller|'''Adoration of the blessed sacrament,''' in the ''Rom. Cath. Ch.'', supreme worship (''latria'') paid to the eucharist. “Catholics pay to the eucharist . . . wherever it may be present that supreme worship which is due to God alone.” ''Cath. Dict.'' (1884), p. 321. Religious communities of women for the ''perpetual adoration of the blessed sacrament'' have been founded at various times, the first by Anne of Austria, mother of Louis XIV.—'''Adoration of the'''}} '''cross,''' in the ''Rom. Cath. Ch.'', that part of the service on Good Friday, following the prayers, in which the cross is exposed to view and “adored” by clergy and people.—'''Adoration of the host,''' in the celebration of the mass, the silent worship paid by the congregation, kneeling, at the elevation of the host. See ''host''<sup>3</sup>.—'''Adoration of the pope,''' a mark of homage paid to the pope immediately after his election, by kissing the golden cross on the sandal worn on his right foot. Cardinals also kiss his right hand, receiving in return the kiss of peace. The ceremony is

6 {{smaller|four times repeated; the first two adorations take place in the conclave itself, the third in the Sistine chapel, and the fourth in St. Peter’s, where the homage of the people is received.}}

'''adoratory''' (a-dōr′a-tō-ri), ''n.''; pl. ''adoratories'' (-riz).   [< ML. ''adōratorium'', explained as “an underground place where the Indians sacrifice to their gods and departed ancestors,” < L. ''adorare'', adore: see ''adore''<sup>1</sup> and ''oratory''.]   A place of worship; especially, a pagan temple or place of sacrifice. [Rare.]

'''adore'''<sup>1</sup> (a-dōr′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''adored'', ppr. ''adoring''.   [< ME. ''adouren'', < OF. ''adourer'', ''adorer'' (earlier ME. ''aouren'', < OF. ''aourer'', ''aürer'', ''aörer''), mod. F. ''adorer'' = Pr. Sp. Pg. ''adorar'' = It. ''adorare'', adore, < L. ''adorare'', speak to, address, beseech, pray to, adore, worship, < ''ad'', to, + ''orare'', speak, pray, < ''os'' (''ōr''-), the mouth: see ''oral''.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To worship; pay supreme reverence to; address in prayer and thanksgiving; pay divine honors to; honor as divine.
{{smaller block|Bishops and priests . . . bearing the host, which he publicly ''adored''.
{{right|''Smollett'', Hist. Eng., an. 1689.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>God shall be all in all. But, all ye gods,
''Adore'' him, who to compass all this dies;
''Adore'' the Son, and honour him as me.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iii. 342.}}}}
'''2.''' To honor and regard in a very high degree; regard with the utmost esteem, love, and respect.
{{smaller block|The people appear ''adoring'' their prince. {{right|''Tatler'', No. 57.}}}}
{{smaller block|Thus, Madam, in the midst of crowds, you reign in solitude; and are ''adored'' with the deepest veneration, that of silence.
{{right|''Dryden'', Ded. of State of Innocence.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>When he who ''adores'' thee has left but the name</poem> Of his faults and his follies behind. {{right|''Moore'', Irish Mel.}}}}

{{smaller block|= '''Syn.''' ''Adore, Worship, Reverence, Venerate, Revere,'' idolize, deify, pay homage to. ''Adore'' and ''worship'', when not applied exclusively to God or gods, are manifestly hyperbolical: as, he ''worshiped'' the ground she trod on. The others seem literal when applied to men, places, or things. ''Adore'' and ''worship'' are applied primarily to acts and words of homage; the others are not. None of them primarily includes the idea of intercessory prayer. ''Adore'' is the noblest of the words. To ''worship'' is to pay homage by outward forms or in customary places: “A man of Ethiopia . . . had come to Jerusalem for to ''worship.''” Acts viii. 27. In the Bible ''worship'' is used to express also extreme manifestations of respect paid to men: “As Peter was coming in, Cornelius met him, and fell down at his feet, and ''worshipped'' him.” Acts x. 25. ''Reverence'' is upon a plane a little different from that of ''venerate'', there being sometimes more fear suggested by the former and more sacredness by the latter. We should ''reverence'' position, ability, and character; we should ''venerate'' old age. ''Revere'' differs from ''reverence'' chiefly in suggesting rather less solemnity or awe.}}

{{smaller block|It [worship] is also an act of the will, whereby the soul ''adores'' and ''reverences'' his majesty. . . . We must ''worship'' God understandingly; it is not else a reasonable service.
{{right|''Charnock'', Attributes.}}}}

<poem>Fall down and dy before her;
So dying live, and living do ''adore'' her.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Spenser'', Sonnets, xiv.}}}}

{{smaller block|I love Quaker ways and Quaker worship, I ''venerate'' the Quaker principles. {{right|''Lamb'', Elia.}}}}

{{smaller block|A foolish world is prone to laugh in public at what in private it ''reveres'' as one of the highest impulses of our nature; namely, love. {{right|''Longfellow'', Hyperion, iii. 8.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To perform an act of worship; be filled with adoration, reverence, or reverential admiration.

{{smaller block|If the stars should appear one night in a thousand years, how would men believe and ''adore!'' {{right|''Emerson'', Nature.}}}}

{{smaller block|Litanies, chanted day and night by ''adoring'' hearts. {{right|''De Quincey'', Secret Societies, i.}}}}

'''adore<sup>2</sup>†''' (a̤-dōr′), ''v. t.''   [A poet. perversion of ''adorn''; perhaps only in the two passages quoted.]   To gild; adorn.
{{smaller block|<poem>Like to the hore
Congealed litle drops which doe the morne ''adore''.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. xi. 46.}}}}
{{smaller block|Armlets for great queens to ''adore''.
{{right|''Fletcher and Massinger'', Elder Brother, iv. 3. (''N. E. D.'')}}}}

'''adorement†''' (a̤-dōr′ment), ''n.'' Adoration; worship.
{{smaller block|''Adorement'' of cats, lizards, and beetles.
{{right|''Sir T. Browne'', Vulg. Err., i. 3.}}}}

'''adorer''' (a̤-dōr′ėr), ''n.''   [< ''adore''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who adores. {{smaller|(''a'') One who worships or honors as divine. (''b'') One who esteems or respects highly; a lover; an admirer.}}
{{smaller block|I profess myself her ''adorer'', not her friend.
{{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, i. 5.}}}}

'''adoring''' (a̤-dōr′ing), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''adore''<sup>1</sup>.]   An act of adoration, or one of homage paid by a lover.
{{smaller block|And soft ''adorings'' from their loves receive.
{{right|''Keats'', Eve of St. Agnes, vi.}}}}

'''adoringly''' (a̤-dōr′ing-li), ''adv.'' With adoration.

'''adorn''' (a̤-dôrn′), ''v. t.''   [< ME. ''adornen'', ''adournen'', < OF. ''adorner'', ''adourner'' (earlier ME. ''aournen'', ''aornen'', < OF. ''aourner'', ''aürner'', ''aörner''), mod. F. ''adorner'' = Sp. Pg. ''adornar'' = It. ''adornare'', < L. ''adornare'', < ''ad'', to, + ''ornare'', deck, beautify: see ornate.]   '''1.''' To beautify or decorate; increase or lend beauty or attractiveness to, as by dress or ornaments; hence, in general, to render pleasing, or more pleasing or attractive; embellish.
{{smaller block|A bride ''adorneth'' herself with her jewels. {{right|Isa. lxi. 10.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Virtue ''adorn’d'' his mind, triumph his brow.</poem>
{{right|''Ford'', Fame’s Memorial.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>He left the name at which the world grew pale,
To point a moral, or ''adorn'' a tale.</poem>
{{right|''Johnson'', Van. of Hum. Wishes, l. 222.}}}}
'''2.''' To display the beauty or excellence of: as, to “''adorn'' the doctrine of God,” Tit. ii. 10.
{{smaller|='''Syn.''' ''Adorn, Ornament, Decorate, Embellish, Beautify, Deck, Array'', grace, garnish, bedeck, set off. (See ''decorate''.) The italicized words, except ''deck'' and ''array'', are expressive of the attempt to add or increase beauty. ''Adorn'' has the most nobleness and spirituality; it is the least external. Garments that ''adorn'' a woman seem a part of her personality and bring out her comeliness; many virtues ''adorn'' his character; the hall was ''adorned'' with the portraits of their ancestors. In these examples, no other word in the list is high enough or near enough to take the place of ''adorn''. ''Ornament'' and ''decorate'' express the addition of something external, which still preserves its separate character and may perhaps be easily removed. ''Ornament'', as kindred to ''adorn'', is nearer to its meaning; ''decorate'' expresses that which is more showy: ''ornamented'' with pictures; the bare walls were ''decorated'' for the occasion with flags and wreaths. Both express the adding of beauty to that which was deficient in it before. ''Embellish'' implies previous beauty, to which luster or brilliancy is added by something which perhaps becomes a part of the original: as, a book ''embellished'' with plates; a style ''embellished'' with figures of speech. The word is sometimes used of over-ornamentation. ''Beautify'' is the most direct in its expression of the general idea. Of the first five words, ''decorate'' is the least often used figuratively; ''decorated'' speech is speech in which the ornaments have no vital connection or harmony with the thought, so that they seem merely ornamental. ''Deck'' is to cover, and hence to cover in a way to please the eye: as, ''decked'' with flowers. ''Array'' is used especially of covering with splendid dress, the meaning being extended from persons to animals, etc.: the fields were ''arrayed'' in green.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>But that which fairest is, but few behold,
Her mind ''adornd'' with vertues manifold.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', Sonnets, xv.}}}}
{{smaller block|A whimsical fashion now prevailed among the ladies, of strangely ''ornamenting'' their faces with abundance of black patches cut into grotesque forms.
{{right|''I. D’Israeli'', Curios. of Lit., I. 311.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Ivy climbs the crumbling hall
To ''decorate'' decay. {{right|''Bailey'', Festus.}}</poem>}}
{{smaller block|We are to dignify to each other the daily needs and offices of man’s life, and ''embellish'' it by courage, wisdom, and unity. {{right|''Emerson'', Friendship.}}}}
{{smaller block|Nature has laid out all her art in ''beautifying'' the face.
{{right|''Addison'', Spectator, No. 98.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And, with new life from sun and kindly showers,
With beauty ''deck'' the meadow and the hill.</poem>
{{right|''Jones Very'', Poems, p. 90.}}}}
{{smaller block|Even Solomon in all his glory was not ''arrayed'' like one of these [lilies]. {{right|Mat. vi. 29.}}}}

'''adorn†''' (a̤-dôrn′), ''n.''   [= It. Sp. ''adorno'', ornament; from the verb.]   Ornament.
{{smaller block|<poem>Her brest all naked, as nett yvory
Without ''adorne'' of gold or silver bright.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., III. xii. 20.}}}}

'''adorn†''' (a̤-dôrn′), ''a.''   [< It. ''adorno'', short form of ''adornato'' (= Sp. Pg. ''adornado''), pp. of ''adornare'', < L. ''adornare'': see ''adornate'', ''adorn'', ''v.'']   Adorned; decorated.
{{smaller block|Made so ''adorn'' for thy delight. {{right|''Milton'', P. L., viii. 576.}}}}

'''adornate†''' (a-dôr′nāt), ''v. t.''   [< L. ''adornatus'', pp. of ''adornare'': see ''adorn'', ''v.'']   To adorn.
{{smaller block|To ''adornate'' gardens with the fairnesse thereof.
{{right|''Frampton'', p. 33.}}}}

'''adornation†''' (ad-ôr-nā′shọn), ''n.''   [< L. as if *''adornatio(n-)'', < ''adornare'', pp. ''adornatus'': see ''adorn'', ''v.'']   Ornament.
{{smaller block|Memory is the soul’s treasury, and thence she hath her garments of ''adornation''.
{{right|''Wits' Commonwealth'', p. 81.}}}}

'''adorner''' (a̤-dôr′nėr), ''n.'' One who adorns.

'''adorning''' (a̤-dôr′ning), ''n.'' Ornament; decoration.
{{smaller block|Whose ''adorning'' let it not be that outward ''adorning'' of plaiting the hair, and of wearing of gold, or of putting on of apparel.
{{right|1 Pet. iii. 3.}}}}

'''adorningly''' (a̤-dôr′ning-li), ''adv.'' By adorning; in an adorning manner.

'''adornment''' (a̤-dôrn′ment), ''n.''   [< ME. ''adournment'', < OF. ''adournement'', ''adornement'' (earlier ME. ''aournement'', ''aornement'', < OF. ''aournement''), mod. F. ''adornement'': see ''adorn'' and ''-ment''.]   An adorning; that which adorns; ornament.
{{smaller block|<poem>I will write all down:
Such and such pictures:—There the window: Such
The ''adornment'' of her bed.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Cymbeline, ii. 2.}}}}

'''adorsed''' (a-dôrst′), ''p. a.''   [Also written ''addorsed'', a restored form of ''adossed'', ''addossed'', < F. ''adossé'', pp. of ''adosser'', set back to back (< ''à'', to, + ''dos'', < L. ''dorsum'', the back), + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.]   Placed back to back. {{smaller|In ''her.'', applied to any two animals, birds, fishes, or other}}
